hook.text: Half the people watching a basketball video missed a gorilla walking through the scene.

buildup.text: Simons and Chabris told viewers to count passes. Their focus locked out everything else.

discovery.text: When attention is fixed on one task, the brain filters out unexpected events entirely.

twist.text: It's not that we chose to ignore the gorilla. Our brain never registered it at all.

climax.text: Focus is a filter. What you attend to defines reality. Everything else vanishes.

punchline.text: You only see what you're looking for.

quiz.question: What caused people to miss the gorilla in the video?
options: The gorilla was too small to see
Their attention was focused on counting passes

details.summary: Inattentional blindness is the failure to perceive clearly visible objects or events when attention is directed elsewhere. The famous invisible gorilla experiment showed that people focused on counting basketball passes completely missed a person in a gorilla suit walking through the scene.
details.whyItMatters: Inattentional blindness reveals that seeing and looking are not the same thing. Critical events can occur in plain sight and go unnoticed when attention is focused elsewhere, with serious implications for safety, security, and decision-making.
takeaways: Focused attention can render clearly visible events completely invisible
The invisible gorilla experiment demonstrated this effect dramatically
Multitasking is especially vulnerable to inattentional blindness

faq.question: How is inattentional blindness different from change blindness?
faq.answer: Inattentional blindness is failing to notice something new that appears while your attention is elsewhere. Change blindness is failing to notice something existing that changes during a disruption. Both reveal limits of visual awareness.

faq.question: Does inattentional blindness affect professionals?
faq.answer: Yes. Radiologists miss unexpected findings on scans when focused on expected abnormalities. Drivers miss pedestrians when texting. Security officers miss contraband when focused on specific threat types. Expertise does not prevent it.
